newsitem.title: UK: BOE inflation view hammers sterling yield curve.
newsitem.headline: BOE inflation view hammers sterling yield curve.

text.p: The sterling yield curve flattened on Tuesday as the market took on board Bank of England comments that interest rates needed to be increased again to hit the official 2.5 percent inflation target.
"The Bank's report was a bit more hawkish than people were expecting but the market is now looking rather more fairly priced," Societe Generale bond strategist Teddy DeWitte said.
LIFFE December short sterling was down seven basis points at 93.07, implying official interest rates of around 6.75 percent by the end of the year, compared with the current 6.25 percent.

Bank of England chief economist Mervyn King spooked short sterling with comments that the Bank would have to "seriously consider raising interest rates in the coming months". DeWitte expects base rates to hit 7.0 percent by the end of year and says that should be the peak.
But if forecasts such as Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's are correct, then the back months of short sterling can expect to fall further.

"We see rates at 7.0 percent by the end of the year, rising to a peak of around 8.0 percent early to mid 1998," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr said. "The Bank of England report, while hawkish, is not overly bearish about interest rates."
March 1998 short sterling was down seven basis points at 92.97 while the June contract was also down seven at 92.89, both implying that rates will rise to around 7.0 percent.
In the gilts market, short-dated bonds eased back on the perception interest rates would rise again while the long end gained support from hopes inflation would be controlled.

In the futures pit, the LIFFE June long gilt contract moved up to an intraday high of 114-23/32, shaking off initial losses, but by the end of the session it was heading back down again in line with other European bonds.
Barr believes further curve-flattening is in prospect.

"The short end will fall as interest rate rises come through and the market is surprised by the extent, while the long end is underpinned by the independence of the Bank of England and signs of convergence among European bonds," he said.

The Treasury ceded control of interest rates to the central bank last week and this attempt at removing political bias from the monetary policy framework has improved demand for long-dated stock on a perception Britain now has a better chance of keeping inflation under control.
But SocGen's DeWitte says the gilt curve is already too flat, while Dresdner Kleinwort Benson economist Steve Scott takes the view that the curve will actually be slightly inverted by next year.
"We'll get a transitional phase of a hump-shaped curve but we see a downward sloping yield curve next year, with short rates at around 7-1/4 percent and long yields about 6-3/4 percent," Scott said.
"If you've got nine people trying to meet an inflation target, they're not going to take any risks," he said, referring to the new monetary policy committee.
If anything, the risk is that rates would be raised by too much, he added.
